_source_note: A small, illustrative subset of documented, publicly reported glacial hazard sites in the Indian Himalaya - not a comprehensive inventory. India's National Disaster Management Authority has identified 56 glacial lakes nationally for real-time monitoring; ISRO/NRSC's 2023 inventory (Rao et al.) catalogued 28,043 glacial lakes >= 0.25 hectares across the Indian Himalayan Region. Every entry below is sourced to specific published reporting; nothing here is estimated or invented. For a real deployment this file should be replaced with the full NDMA/NRSC monitored-lake inventory - see glacierwatch/tools/watchlist.py docstring.

regional_context.total_glacial_lakes_indian_himalaya: 28,043 lakes >= 0.25 ha, per ISRO/NRSC inventory (Rao et al., 2023)
regional_context.nationally_monitored_at_risk_lakes: 56 lakes identified by India's National Disaster Management Authority for real-time early-warning monitoring
regional_context.sikkim_susceptibility_tiers: Updated GLOF susceptibility mapping of Sikkim's moraine-dammed lakes: 1 very-high, 8 high, 22 medium, 56 low, 18 very-low risk (ScienceDirect, 'Increasing risk of glacial lake outburst flood in Sikkim, Eastern Himalaya under climate warming', 2024)
regional_context.sutlej_basin_lake_count: 2,292 glacial lakes mapped in the Sutlej basin alone, spanning Himachal Pradesh and Jammu & Kashmir (The News Himachal, Aug 2026)

sites.name: Gepang Gath Lake
static_risk_factors: Lake area grew 176% in 33 years: 36.49 ha (1989) -> 101.30 ha (2022), one of the fastest-growing lakes in the region
Parent glacier (Gepang Gath Glacier) in sustained negative mass balance: -0.90 m water-equivalent/year, 2015-2023
Parent glacier has retreated ~2.76 km since 1962, current retreat rate ~53 m/year

Moraine-dammed lake; NRSC and Journal of Geophysical Research: Earth Surface (Sattar et al., 2023) studies have modeled artificial lake-level lowering as a mitigation option, indicating the dam is not considered self-stabilizing
sites.downstream_exposure: Worst-case modeling: floodwaters could reach Sissu village in ~21 minutes of a breach, at speeds up to 43 km/h and depths up to 20 m. Threatens 34 settlements, ~204 ha of cultivable land, 57 bridges, 106 km of road, the Manali-Leh National Highway, and the Atal Tunnel approach.
sources: Down To Earth, 'How big a threat is the expanding Ghepan Lake above Sissu village in Himachal Pradesh' (2026)
Deccan Herald, 'Himachal Pradesh's Sissu sits on time bomb as expanding glacial lake threatens 34 settlements' (2026)
Sattar et al., 'Modeling Potential Glacial Lake Outburst Flood Process Chains and Effects From Artificial Lake-Level Lowering at Gepang Gath Lake, Indian Himalaya', JGR: Earth Surface (2023)

sites.name: Samudra Tapu Glacial Lake
sites.static_risk_classification: NRSC has published a formal GLOF Risk Assessment report on this lake; it is monitored due to sustained rapid expansion.
static_risk_factors: Proglacial lake fed by Samudra Tapu Glacier, the second-largest glacier in the upper Chandra basin
1971-2014: lake expanded 1,889 m linearly and ~1 km^2 in area
Over the same period, lake volume grew roughly 20-fold: from ~3.4 million m^3 to ~67.7 million m^3
Continued feeder-glacier melt identified in the literature as the primary driver of the volume increase
sites.downstream_exposure: Located in the upper Chandra basin, Lahaul and Spiti - downstream communities and infrastructure along the Chandra/Chenab basin are exposed; precise inundation modeling is in NRSC's formal risk assessment report, not reproduced here.
sources: Kulkarni & Dhar, 'Recession of Samudra Tapu glacier, Chandra River basin, Himachal Pradesh'
NRSC, 'GLOF Risk Assessment of Samudra Tapu Glacial Lake' (Bhuvan NHP-FS report repository)

sites.name: South Lhonak Lake
sites.static_risk_classification: GLOF occurred 4 October 2023 - included here as the region's canonical case study, not an active site
static_risk_factors: Had been formally identified as one of Sikkim's 14 potentially dangerous glacial lakes since at least 2019, before it breached
An early-warning system had been installed but was non-operational due to extreme weather at the exact moment the lake failed

Failure mechanism: a 14.7 million m3 landslide from the lake's lateral moraine plunged into the lake, generating a ~20 m tsunami wave that overtopped and breached the frontal moraine, releasing ~50 million m3 of water down the Teesta valley
Flood traveled 50 km downstream, killed 42 people, left 70+ missing, destroyed 30+ bridges across four Sikkim districts, and destroyed the Teesta III hydropower dam
sites.downstream_exposure: Already realized in 2023 - included as a reference case for calibrating this tool's risk criteria and as a reminder that a known, documented hazard with a partially built early-warning system still resulted in major loss of life when the EWS lost power at a critical moment.
sources: Down To Earth, 'The 2023 Sikkim disaster exposes growing risk of GLOFs in a warming Himalaya'
Science, 'The Sikkim flood of October 2023: Drivers, causes, and impacts of a multihazard cascade' (2024)

sites.name: Chorabari Lake (Gandhi Sarovar)
sites.static_risk_classification: Moraine breached 17 June 2013 - lake did not reform (moraine largely washed away). Included only as the reference case used to calibrate this tool's extreme-rainfall trigger threshold, not as an active site.
static_risk_factors: 17 June 2013: more than 315 mm of rainfall in the surrounding catchment combined with rapid glacier melt raised lake levels until the moraine dam failed
The lake drained completely in 5-10 minutes once the breach began, sending a debris- and boulder-laden surge down the Mandakini valley into Kedarnath town
One of the deadliest disasters in Uttarakhand's history; thousands of pilgrims and residents were killed
sites.downstream_exposure: Already realized in 2013. Retained in this watchlist specifically because its documented rainfall trigger (>315 mm in a short window, combined with rapid melt) is the single most concrete, citable precipitation threshold available for calibrating this tool's heavy-rainfall flag - see glacierwatch/tools/weather.py.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Chorabari Lake' and '2013 North India floods'
Manchalamushafir, 'Chorabari Lake Kedarnath (Gandhi Sarovar) - Trek & History'
